Dimension reduction¶

Problem: ambient dimension of dataset is very high

Manifold hypothesis: dataset lies on a lower dimensional submanifold.

Question: How to find this submanifold?

General paradigms: feature selection and feature extraction

-Feature selection: want to select a subset for features (i.e. variables and predicted quantities) in order to remove redundant and irrelevant features.

-Feature extraction: combine several features into one in order to reduce the number of features while minimizing information loss

Three techniques we want to look into further

-Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

-t-distributed stochastic neighborhood embedding (t-sne)

-Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)

(Thank you to Davide Gurnari for his slides on the subject!)

Principal Component Analysis¶

PCA is a linear dimensionality reduction technique that finds the axes (aka "principal components") along which the variance in the data is maximized.

It then projects data onto these principal components to reduce dimensionality while retaining as much of the original variability as possible.

Let XX be a n×pn×p (centered) data matrix.

The covariance matrix is given by C=X⊤X/(n−1)C=X⊤X/(n−1) (Actually this is abuse of notation, but X⊤X/(n−1)X⊤X/(n−1) is proportional to the actual covariance matrix).

It is a symmetric matrix and so it can be diagonalized: C=VLV⊤,C=VLV⊤, where VV is a matrix of eigenvectors (each column is an eigenvector) and LL is a diagonal matrix with eigenvalues λiλi in the decreasing order on the diagonal.

The eigenvectors are called principal axes or principal directions of the data.

The jj-th principal component is given by jj-th column of XVXV. The coordinates of the ii-th data point in the new PC space are given by the ii-th row of XVXV.

SVD and PCA¶

The singular value decomposition (SVD) of XX is

X=USVTX=USVT

where UU is a unitary matrix (with columns called left singular vectors), SS is the diagonal matrix of singular values sisi and VV columns are called right singular vectors.

Therefore

C=VSUTUSVT/(n−1)=VS2n−1VT,C=VSUTUSVT/(n−1)=VS2n−1VT,

right singular vectors VV are principal directions (eigenvectors) and that singular values are related to the eigenvalues of covariance matrix via λi=s2i/(n−1)λi=si2/(n−1).

Principal components are given by XV=USVTV=USXV=USVTV=US.

t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding¶

t-SNE minimizes the divergence between probability distributions that represent pairwise similarities in high-dimensional and low-dimensional spaces.

1. Compute Pairwise Similarities in High-Dimensional Space¶

For each point xixi, the probability that xjxj is a neighbor of xixi

pj|i=exp(−∥xi−xj∥2/2σ2i)∑k≠iexp(−∥xi−xk∥2/2σ2i)pj|i=exp⁡(−‖xi−xj‖2/2σi2)∑k≠iexp⁡(−‖xi−xk‖2/2σi2)

The variance σiσi is adapted to the density of the data: smaller values of σiσi are used in denser regions.

The joint probability pijpij is then computed as:

pij=pj|i+pi|j2Npij=pj|i+pi|j2N

2. Compute Pairwise Similarities in Low-Dimensional Space¶

In the low-dimensional space, the similarity between pair of points is defined via a Student’s t-distribution with one degree of freedom:

qij=(1+∥yi−yj∥2)−1∑k≠l(1+∥yk−yl∥2)−1qij=(1+‖yi−yj‖2)−1∑k≠l(1+‖yk−yl‖2)−1

The t-distribution has heavier tails than a Gaussian. Less similar pairs are penalized less heavily on the lower-dimensional embedding.

3. Minimize the Kullback-Leibler Divergence¶

t-SNE minimizes the difference between the high-dimensional probability distribution pijpij and the low-dimensional distribution qijqij using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence:

C=∑i≠jpijlogpijqijC=∑i≠jpijlog⁡pijqij

Hyperparameters¶

The σiσi are directly related to perplexity, which controls how many "neighbors" each point considers when measuring similarity.

The relationship between σiσi and perplexity is established through an iterative process to find the right σiσi for each data point that matches the target perplexity.

What is Perplexity?¶

Perplexity can be thought of as a smooth measure of the number of nearest neighbors considered for each point. It balances between local structure (small perplexity) and global structure (large perplexity).

The perplexity is defined as:

Perplexity=2H(Pi)Perplexity=2H(Pi)

Where H(Pi)H(Pi) is the Shannon entropy of the conditional probability distribution PiPi:

H(Pi)=−∑jpj|ilog2pj|iH(Pi)=−∑jpj|ilog2⁡pj|i

Relationship between σiσi and Perplexity:¶

For each data point xixi, t-SNE searches for the value of σiσi that makes the entropy H(Pi)H(Pi) approximately equal to the log of the target perplexity:

H(Pi)≈log2(Perplexity)H(Pi)≈log2⁡(Perplexity)

Thus, the correct σiσi ensures that the conditional probability distribution pj|ipj|i has the desired "spread" of neighbors to match the perplexity.

  • Small σiσi → Distribution is very narrow → Few neighbors have high probability (low perplexity).
  • Large σiσi → Distribution is broad → Many neighbors have similar probabilities (high perplexity).

How t-SNE Finds σiσi:¶

t-SNE uses binary search on σiσi for each data point xixi to ensure the perplexity matches the target value:

  1. Compute the conditional probabilities pj|ipj|i for an initial σiσi.
  2. Calculate the entropy H(Pi)H(Pi).
  3. Adjust σiσi using binary search until H(Pi)≈log2(Perplexity)H(Pi)≈log2⁡(Perplexity).

Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection¶

UMAP can be used similarly to t-SNE but it claims to capture more of the global structure with superior run time performance.

The algorithm is founded on three assumptions about the data:

  1. The data is uniformly distributed on a Riemannian manifold;
  2. The Riemannian metric is locally constant (or can be approximated as such);
  3. The manifold is locally connected.

Graph Construction in High-Dimensional Space¶

UMAP first builds a weighted graph in the high-dimensional space:

  1. k-Nearest Neighbors:
    For each data point xixi, UMAP finds its kk-nearest neighbors {xj}{xj} using a chosen distance metric.

The unit ball centered around each point is given by it's k-NN.

  1. Fuzzy Graph Representation:
    Instead of using fixed edges between points, UMAP uses a fuzzy set to represent local relationships.

    The edge weight wijwij between two points xixi and xjxj is given by:

    wij=exp(−max(0,d(xi,xj)−ρi)σi)wij=exp⁡(−max(0,d(xi,xj)−ρi)σi) Where:

    • d(xi,xj)d(xi,xj) is the distance between points xixi and xjxj.
    • ρiρi is the distance to the nearest neighbor of xixi, ensuring no zero distances dominate.
    • σiσi controls the local scaling and is chosen to balance the neighborhood size.

Optimization in Low-Dimensional Space¶

In the low-dimensional space, the probability qijqij of two points yiyi and yjyj being close is modeled using a Student’s t-distribution.

UMAP tries to minimize the difference between the fuzzy graph in high-dimensional space and the corresponding fuzzy graph in low-dimensional space by minimizingthe following cross-entropy loss:

C=∑i≠jwijlog(wijqij)+(1−wij)log(1−wij1−qij)C=∑i≠jwijlog⁡(wijqij)+(1−wij)log⁡(1−wij1−qij)

Hyperparameters¶

n_neighbors: Controls the size of the local neighborhood used for graph construction.

  • Low values → Focuses on fine detail (local structure).
  • High values → Focuses on broader patterns (global structure).

min_dist: Controls how tightly UMAP packs points together.

  • Low values → Clusters are tighter.
  • High values → Clusters are more spread out.

Metric vs. topological approaches¶

So far, we have considered mathematical models, clustering, and dimension reduction.¶

Mathematical models: if appropriate, describe the data best

Problems:

  • correct model is difficult to find
  • for complex models: combinatorial explosion
  • Danger of overfitting
  • not stable

Metric vs. topological approaches¶

Dimension reduction: allows at least visualization, might counteract curse of dimensionality

Problems:

  • often no theoretical guarantees for preservation of relevant features
  • hard to evaluate without ground truth

Clustering: groups relevant data points together, provides methods of evaluation

Problems:

  • relatively simple, only connected components
  • can we keep more information?

Geometric approximation and topological invariants¶

New approach: Try to approximate shapes rather than fitting them precisely

→→ leads to more fuzzy approximations

→→ Use homotopy invariants to reduce to the relevant information

Background¶

There are various types of geometric objects we could use to approximate data

Types of geometric objects¶

(Smooth/differentiable) Manifolds (simplicial/cubical/CW) Complexes topological/metric spaces
-locally given by parametrizations/solutions to differentiable equations -result of successive gluing instructions -given by a set of points +topology/metric
-locally Euclidean ≅Rn≅Rn -built out of simple building blocks: simplices/cubes/cells -local neighborhoods might be complicated
-have chart transfer maps/an atlas -have skeletal filtration -no canonical decomposition
-may be embedded in RnRn or abstract -may be geometrically embedded or abstract -no canonical embedding
-notion of dimension coming from RnRn -notion of dimension coming from building blocks Δn,In,DnΔn,In,Dn -no general notion of dimension
-tools from differential topology/geometry -tools from combinatorial topology/geometry -tools from point set topology
-to computers only directly accessible via parametrizations/systems of differentiable equations -to computers accessible via various graph structures (simplex tree/face poset/cliques in the 1-skeleton/...) -in this generality, only finite spaces are directly accessible to computers

Abstract spaces:

advantages: do not have to deal with parametrizations/gluing maps
disadvantages: have no idea what they look like

Topological spaces¶

Definition: Let XX be a set. A topology on XX is a collection ττ of subsets U⊆XU⊆X such that

  1. ∅,X∈τ∅,X∈τ
  1. U1,…,Un∈τ⇒⋂i=1,…,nUi∈τU1,…,Un∈τ⇒⋂i=1,…,nUi∈τ
  1. {Ui}i∈I∈τ⇒⋃i∈IUi∈τ{Ui}i∈I∈τ⇒⋃i∈IUi∈τ

The UiUi are called open sets.

Metrics versus Topology¶

Metric spaces are topological spaces:

The ϵϵ-balls generate a topology via arbitrary unions.

How do we understand topological spaces?

Via maps between them!

Definition

A map between topological spaces f:(X,τX)→(Y,τY)f:(X,τX)→(Y,τY) is called continuous if for all U∈τY, f−1(U)∈τXU∈τY, f−1(U)∈τX.

A map is called a homeomorphism if it is continuous, bijective, and its inverse is continuous.

Criteria for continuity¶

If ff is a map between metric spaces, then continuity is equivalent to ϵ−δϵ−δ continuity and sequence-continuity.

If ff is differentiable, then ff is continuous.

For topological purposes:¶

Definition:

A metric is called finite is supx,y∈Xd(x,y)<∞supx,y∈Xd(x,y)<∞.

Two metric are called equivalent if they induce the same topology.

Proposition:

Every metric d(x,y)d(x,y) is equivalent to a finite one.

Idea of proof.

Check that

d′(x,y):=d(x,y)1+d(x,y)d′(x,y):=d(x,y)1+d(x,y)

is bounded by 1 and equivalent to d(x,y)d(x,y).

Homotopy equivalence¶

Definition:

Let f,g:X→Yf,g:X→Y be continuous maps. We say that ff is homotopic to gg, denoted by f≃gf≃g, if there is a continuous map h:X×[0,1]→Yh:X×[0,1]→Y such that h|X×{0}=fh|X×{0}=f and h|X×{1}=gh|X×{1}=g.

Definition:

Let X,YX,Y be topological spaces. We say that XX and YY are homotopy equivalent, denoted by X≃YX≃Y, if there are continuous maps f:X→Yf:X→Y and g:Y→Xg:Y→X such that fg≃idYfg≃idY and gf≃idXgf≃idX.
